title: Visa Sponsorship: What Employers Actually Mean When They Say No
excerpt: It is rarely a judgement about you. Understanding the constraint turns a wall into a map.
content:
You find the role. You match the requirements almost perfectly. You get to the bottom of the advert and there it is: We are unable to offer visa sponsorship for this position.

It feels personal. It is not. But understanding what is actually happening behind that sentence changes how you search, and it turns a wall into a map.

Sponsorship is a licence, not a decision

Here is the thing most applicants never learn. In the UK, an employer cannot simply decide to sponsor you because they like you. They must already hold a sponsor licence from the Home Office. Getting one costs money, takes months, and commits the company to ongoing record keeping and compliance duties that a small firm may have no capacity for.

So when a company says it cannot sponsor, the honest translation is usually one of two things. Either they do not hold a licence at all, which is true of the large majority of small and medium employers. Or they hold one but have not been allocated the certificate for this particular role.

Neither is a judgement about you. A hiring manager who loved your CV genuinely cannot override it. Arguing, or offering to work for less, or promising to sort your own paperwork, does not help, because the constraint is not in their gift.

Search the licence, not the job board

This is the single most useful thing in this article, and almost nobody does it.

The UK government publishes the full register of licensed sponsors. It is a public list of every organisation permitted to sponsor a worker, searchable, updated regularly, and free. Similar transparency exists in other systems in different forms.

Which means you can invert the whole process. Rather than applying to a hundred jobs and discovering at the end which ones were ever possible, start from the register. Filter for your sector and your region. You now have a list of companies where sponsorship is at least on the table. Go and look at their careers pages directly.

Being on the register does not guarantee they will sponsor you for a given role. It does guarantee that they can, which removes the most common reason applications die.

The salary threshold nobody mentions

Even with a licensed employer, sponsored roles generally have to pay above a minimum threshold, and there is usually a separate going rate for the specific occupation. Your offer has to clear whichever is higher.

This quietly explains a lot of rejections. A junior role at a licensed company may simply pay below the floor, so sponsorship is impossible regardless of how much they want you. It also explains why aiming slightly more senior sometimes works better than aiming lower. The instinct to apply for something easier to get can move you further from eligibility, not closer.

Thresholds change. Check the current figures on the official government pages rather than trusting a blog post, including this one.

Routes that do not need an employer at all

Sponsorship is one door. It is not the building.

  • Points based systems. Canada and Australia assess you directly on age, education, language and experience. No employer required to begin.
  • Study routes. A degree abroad often carries post study work rights, which converts you into a local hire and removes the sponsorship problem entirely.
  • Talent and specialist routes. Several countries have visas for people with demonstrable achievement in a field, endorsed by a recognised body rather than a company.
  • Working remotely for foreign employers. Not migration, but it pays in a stronger currency and builds exactly the international track record that makes the other routes easier later.

How to ask without wasting anyone’s time

If an advert is silent on sponsorship, ask early and plainly. One short message before you invest in a long application:

I am very interested in this role and believe I meet the requirements. Before I apply, could you confirm whether the position is open to candidates who would require sponsorship? I want to be respectful of your time either way.

A no costs you two minutes instead of two evenings. A yes tells you to put real effort in. Recruiters generally appreciate the directness, because the alternative is discovering the mismatch at offer stage, which is worse for everybody.

None of this makes the process easy. It is genuinely hard, and the rules shift. But most of the exhaustion people feel comes from applying blind into a system whose constraints are, unusually, published in public. Read the constraints first. Then spend your energy where the door is already open.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
